title: OpenAI launches MedChemBench: GPT-6.2 Astra scores 84.5% on medicinal chemistry reasoning
summary: Medicinal chemists face one question every day: which compound to synthesize and test next. OpenAI's new MedChemBench uses 99 problems drawn from published research to test whether AI can connect molecular structures with experimental evidence and decide which compound to test next. The top performer, GPT-6.2 Astra, earned 84.5% of available credit at xhigh, but compound selection and numerical prediction remain weak points.
ai_summary: OpenAI released MedChemBench on November 20, 2026, a benchmark for medicinal chemistry reasoning. It uses 99 problems from published research to test whether AI can connect molecular structure, experimental evidence, and the next compound to test. At the xhigh setting, the highest reasoning level shared by all models, GPT-6.2 Astra earned 84.5% overall, ahead of GPT-6 Astra at 83.3% and GPT-5.6 Sol at 58.2%. By component, Astra was strong at reconstructing molecular structures with 95.4%, but compound selection and numerical prediction earned only about half. For scientists who want to use AI in drug discovery, this shows where models are strong and weak. OpenAI is clear, though, that this does not mean models can discover new drugs, prior exposure to public sources cannot be ruled out, and each problem was answered once with no tools or feedback.
brief: MedChemBench contains 99 problems drawn from 117 papers and patents, covering 761 distinct molecular structures.
xhigh total scores: GPT-6.2 Astra 84.5%, GPT-6 Astra 83.3%, GPT-6.1 Sol 82.0%, GPT-5.6 Sol 58.2%.
Astra scored 95.4% on reconstructing molecular structures, but only about half on compound selection and numerical prediction.
On the 18-atom ring spatial reasoning problem, GPT-6 Astra got all 10 attempts right; the GPT-5.6 models got all 10 wrong.

sections.h: What MedChemBench is: a set of medicinal chemistry reasoning problems

blocks.p: OpenAI released MedChemBench on November 20, 2026. It is not a drug-finding AI per se; it is a benchmark that checks whether a model can match “what a molecule looks like” with “what experiments measured” and then decide which compound to try next. Medicinal chemistry is the discipline of designing, modifying, and evaluating compounds as medicines.

The hardest part of this work is trade-offs: improving one property often makes another worse. A compound can act strongly against a disease-related protein but still be poorly absorbed or break down too quickly in the body. Working medicinal chemists design, synthesize, and test a series of related compounds, then decide where to go next. MedChemBench tests whether AI has that layer of reasoning: connecting structural changes to experimental evidence.

sections.h: What four abilities does it test?

blocks.p: MedChemBench splits scoring into four categories. In most problems, the model receives the context available at a given point in a research project: the biological target, the researchers' goals, the compounds studied so far, and selected experimental findings. It is then scored on four dimensions:

list: Molecular structure: assemble the molecule from the chemical drawings and groups provided, with correct atom connectivity and stereochemistry (the spatial arrangement of atoms).
Scientific reasoning: explanations must be supported by evidence provided in the problem, such as why one compound was chosen over another.
Ranking and selection: compound rankings and choices must meet the requirements stated in the problem.
Property prediction: predicted values and categories should be close to the results reported in the source literature, including measured and calculated molecular properties.

sections.h: Reading the scores: who got what

blocks.p: At the xhigh setting, the highest reasoning-effort setting shared by all models and one that makes models reason more, the top total score was GPT-6.2 Astra with 84.5% of available credit, followed by GPT-6 Astra at 83.3%, GPT-6.1 Sol at 82.0%, GPT-6.1 Terra at 75.1%, and GPT-5.6 Sol with only 58.2%.

blocks.p: Here 84.5% means “percentage of available credit,” not a simple accuracy rate: some problems award partial credit, with more credit the closer predictions are to measured values. The same model can also score differently at other reasoning settings: GPT-6 Astra reached 83.8% at max, the highest reasoning-effort setting. Figure 2 in the original plots 9 models and 51 model-by-reasoning-setting combinations, with output tokens on the horizontal axis. The trend is that more reasoning leads to higher scores, but clear gaps between models remain.

sections.h: A concrete challenge: block the target, cross the cell barrier, and avoid fast metabolism

blocks.p: One MedChemBench problem is drawn from PRMT5 inhibitor research. PRMT5 is a protein studied in cancer drug discovery. The model receives molecular structures and earlier experimental results and must predict three properties for three related compounds at once: how strongly they block PRMT5 in cells, how readily they cross the cell barrier, and how quickly they break down in a liver-enzyme assay.

The problem withholds the later experiments, which showed a trade-off: compound 23 blocked PRMT5 at a lower concentration, but compound 24 crossed the cell barrier more readily and broke down more slowly in the liver-enzyme assay. In other words, no single compound won on all three properties. That is the central difficulty of medicinal chemistry: stronger activity against a target does not mean better permeability or slower breakdown.

Scoring checks whether the model reconstructs molecular structures correctly and how close its predictions are to measured values; closer predictions earn more partial credit. Measurements already supplied in the problem must also be reproduced correctly.

sections.h: Before any reasoning, the model has to get the molecule right

blocks.p: Before discussing properties, the model must first identify the molecule correctly. Chemical drawings encode atom connectivity, ring structures, and stereochemistry. MedChemBench checks whether the model preserves that information when reconstructing molecules.

One problem asks the model to assemble a molecule from a central structure and two attached groups while preserving an 18-atom ring. At the xhigh setting, GPT-6 Astra answered all ten attempts correctly; GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-5.6 Luna failed all ten. In the examples, GPT-5.6 Sol produced a 15-atom ring, and GPT-5.6 Luna split the molecule into two disconnected fragments. These errors change the identity of the molecule being analyzed.

This is also Astra's strongest area: structure reconstruction earned 95.4% of available credit at xhigh. By contrast, compound selection and numerical prediction earned only about half. In other words, the model can “see the molecule clearly and explain the reasoning” but still has a lot of ground to make up in “choosing the right next compound and getting the numbers right.”

list: Whether MedChemBench's question bank and scoring scripts are fully public and downloadable: the original only links to the paper, without saying when or how to access them.
Whether the benchmark will become an OpenAI product or API: the original doesn't mention it.
How models from other companies perform: this evaluation covered 11 GPT models only, with no external-model comparisons.
Whether the models' training data included these papers and patents: OpenAI explicitly says it cannot rule out that the models have seen these public sources before.
Whether these scores represent real-world drug-finding ability in the lab: OpenAI explicitly says they do not establish that models can discover new drugs or improve experimental decisions.
Whether each answer was a single attempt and whether tools were involved: the original states each response was a single attempt with no tools, feedback, or new experiments.

blocks.p: Value: for teams in medicinal chemistry, computational chemistry, or anyone trying to judge whether AI can now help choose compounds, MedChemBench offers a fairly concrete four-part checkup. Molecular structure, scientific reasoning, ranking and selection, and property prediction are scored separately, which is more useful than a single overall number.

Cost: it tests reasoning on historical literature rather than a real drug-discovery process; the questions may have been seen by the models, and every answer is a single attempt with no tools. Treating it as proof that AI can replace chemists would clearly overstate what it shows.

list: If you are a medicinal chemistry researcher: use it as a capability map, and focus on the two weak areas, selection and property prediction.

If you are an AI team or benchmark author: this breakdown of strengths in structure and reasoning and weaknesses in selection and prediction is a useful starting point for future improvements and comparisons.
If you only care whether AI will find new drugs soon: the safer conclusion is not yet. The results show progress in reasoning, not that AI can discover new drugs.
